title: Ang 318–323: Gauri ki Var M5

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ang 300: the daily routine, from early waking to every breath and bite. Today is test day.

How was your day? Usually the answer is a score: good if it went your way, bad if it didn't. Today is Simran's driving test, 10:40, her dad in the waiting room, Maya texting from school, Bebe's Sukhmani path done before breakfast. Pass, and it's a great day. Fail, and it's the worst one of the year. That's the math, anyway. Guru Arjan's ballad in Gauri, from Ang 318, works it out differently.
screen: `HOW WAS YOUR DAY? A SCORE.` → `10:40, THE TEST.` → `A DIFFERENT MATH.`

segments.voice: The question is old: what makes a day good? Guru Arjan's ballad sets short saloks of his own between its stanzas, and one of them answers, in paraphrase: Nanak, beautiful is the day when God comes to mind; cursed is even a fine season when the Supreme Lord is forgotten. So a day's worth has nothing to do with the result. A day is beautiful when the Lord comes to mind. A perfect spring is a loss if you spent it forgetting. Here's the unity thread. The Psalms, sung by Jews and Christians, have a line that leans the same way. In the King James Version: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." Shared ground: the goodness of a day comes from God, not from the scoreboard. Two old songs, from two families of faith, turned toward the same sky. And one honest difference. The psalm calls the day good because the Lord made it, and calls for joy in it. The salok puts the weight on the person: the same day is beautiful or wasted depending on whether God comes to mind. One looks to the day's maker; the other to the heart that remembers. Neither cancels the other.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A DAY GOOD?` · `THE DAY GOD COMES TO MIND.` · `PSALM 118: THE DAY THE LORD MADE.` · `THE MAKER, OR THE REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `ARJAN'S BALLAD.`

segments.voice: Count back through today, or yesterday if today has barely started, and stop at each moment something good came to mind: a face, a meal, a kindness, a breath that came easy. Don't score them. Just count them, one finger at a time, and rest on the last one.
Ang 318: where Guru Arjan's ballad in Gauri begins, with saloks of his own between the stanzas.
Your line: arjan's ballad. Beautiful is the day when God comes to mind, whatever the score says. Go well.

notes: v3 storyline (days 1471–1484): Simran is learning to drive in the yard of her dad Harjit's trucking company, with the test at the end of the second week. Bebe Jaswant appears once a week (1474, 1480); Maya, her best friend, comes in and out; paced over two weeks, no overnight turnarounds. Day 1483: test day; her dad waits, Maya texts, Bebe's Sukhmani path done that morning. The result comes in day 1484's hook.

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared ground with the Jewish and Christian Psalms (Psalm 118:24, KJV), in that text's own words; one honest difference (the day's maker vs. the remembering heart). Ranking none. Confirm a Jewish and a Christian reader would find it fair.
The salok 'naanak soee dinas suhaavarraa jit prabh aavai chit' is placed in Gauri ki Var M5 at Ang 318 from memory; confirm. The heading's tune instruction is not mentioned, on purpose.
